en: Commentary on the *Ten Doubts*, with Preface.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai. (Annotated by the Śramaṇa Chengyu; Prefaced by the Śramaṇa Zanning. The Preface states:
Now, when one speaks of the realm of the Great Man, it is ultimately impossible to value or believe [it]; for it is indeed a teaching that is difficult to believe.

It is like observing the majesty and nobility of a sovereign and sighing, "I shall certainly never be able to draw near him. Yet, through sudden reliance upon another power, one brings that person to one's very side;
this is the verification of other-power (*tara-shiki*). Only the Great Master of Wisdom was capable of this.

Having ascended to the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), he let out a lion’s roar, the sound of which was heard everywhere—terrible and difficult to comprehend, comparable to the guidance of a great minister.

It is said that when one does not embody the Way, how can the paths of other lands be opened? Therefore, the Venerable Chengyue of Wushan wielded a brush as vast as the heavens, and from it emerged these chapters and verses.

By examining the text, one may perceive the meaning without waiting for the day’s end. May those who are lost children be led back to their father’s house. There is no need for further words of praise;
this person has dedicated themselves solely to the practice of Pure Land, guiding and encouraging the multitudes so that the ignorant... [may attain enlightenment].
To praise this gateway and precede the discourse with a preface concerning my own rebirth in that land, I now first set forth the journey.

This is the *Commentary on the Treatise on the Ten Doubts Concerning the Pure Land*, composed in the eighth year of the Taiping Xingguo era of the Great Song, in the month of the Earth-Hare (*chūnwèi*).

The realm of the Buddhas is neither land nor body; yet, in accordance with the capacities of various beings, it is provisionally established as the "dependent" (the environment) and the "correct" (the body).

To summarize the holy teachings throughout the entire dispensation, they generally clarify four lands and three bodies: first, the Land of Common Dwelling of the Defiled and the Pure, where ordinary beings and sages dwell together;

second, the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, where those of the Three Vehicles dwell having completely severed the afflictions of the paths of seeing and cultivation; third, the Land of True Reward Free from Obstruction... [and so forth].

Regarding the classification of lands, the fundamental ignorance and afflictions are severed at their root. Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body dwell in the four lands of the eternally quiescent light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-śubha-kṣetra*).

As for the land inhabited solely by the Dharma-body of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), when these two types of lands are contrasted: the Sahā world is the defiled land of common residence (*sahā-loka-sāmānya-vāsa*), while the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is the pure land of common residence.
This is because the latter, though lacking the three evil realms, possesses both human and celestial beings. One master elucidates these four lands.

First is the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), the abode of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Second is the land of self-enjoyment, the abode of the self-enjoyment reward-body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*);
these two lands are identical to the aforementioned Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-praśānta-prabhāsa*).

Third is the land of other-enjoyment, the abode of the other-enjoyment reward-body (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*), which manifests a portion of subtle marks for Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward; this is identical to the aforementioned Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-bhūmi*).
The fourth is the land of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is the dwelling place of the transformation lands.

When it manifests a portion of coarse characteristics for bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and for ordinary beings of the two vehicles (*yāna*), it refers to the aforementioned "convenient" land where the defiled and pure coexist, the land of the two vehicles.

Now, the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*) consists of both the "enjoyment for others" (*parasaṃbhoga*) and the "transformation" lands; this is because bodhisattvas who have reached the stages perceive it as the land of the enjoyment for others.
Bodhisattvas of the past, followers of the two vehicles, and ordinary beings behold the land of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*).
The merits and bliss of that land are beyond description; thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:

"Even if one were to pass through immeasurable kalpas, using immeasurable tongues, with each tongue producing immeasurable sounds to praise its merits, one could not exhaust them. If one can rely upon this sūtra...
Those who cultivate the three kinds of pure conduct and the sixteen sublime contemplations, or even achieve the ten recitations at the moment of death, will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Yet, deluded people do not believe this; they frequently give rise to doubt and slander, thereby harming themselves and others.

For this reason, the Great Master Zhiwei briefly set forth the "Ten Doubts," investigating and deliberating upon them through subtle and profound meanings to resolve the net of doubts; thus, it is called the *Jingtu* (Pure Land).
*The Treatise on the Ten Doubts*.

First Doubt. Question: Since all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their vocation, if they wish to rescue and deliver sentient beings, they should simply vow to be born within the triple world, amidst the five turbidities and the three paths of suffering.

Regarding the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*): first is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). "Eon" refers to a period of time; it is called a "turbidity" because the four other turbidities gather together during that eon, specifically at the time of its decline.
Thus, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "From eighty thousand years down to thirty thousand years, there was as yet no turbidity;

it was only when the lifespan reached twenty thousand years that the five turbidities first began. Second is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), which refers to the existence of greed and so forth.

1. The turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*) refers to the five dull underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely: hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and [the remaining two]. Because of these, they are called "turbidity. 2. The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*) refers to taking birth within the six realms of existence.

This conventional designation is established based on the karmic retribution resulting from views and pride; therefore, it is called "turbidity. 3. The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) consists of the five sharp underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):

the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Together with the sixty-two [views], these constitute the turbidity of views.

Because they are perceived, they are called "corruptions. The fifth is the corruption of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), which refers to the continuity of form and mind that constitutes life; when this life is short, it is called a corruption.
Why should one who seeks to save suffering sentient beings instead seek birth in a Pure Land for their own personal peace?
To abandon sentient beings in this way is to lack great compassion; it is solely for the sake of self-benefit and acts as an obstacle to the path to Bodhi.
The answer is: There are two kinds of bodhisattvas. First, those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

these are truly the ones to be questioned. Second, those bodhisattvas who, though they have not yet attained the patience of non-arising, have returned to the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) since their initial resolve;
such individuals must always remain inseparable from the Buddha, and only when their power of patience is perfected are they fit to dwell within the three realms during an evil age.

Regarding the vow of this bodhisattva to rescue suffering sentient beings from within [saṃsāra], it is said that one first realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and subsequently delivers sentient beings;
thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "An ordinary person bound by all fetters..."

"Bondage" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are able to entangle and bind a person; because ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) possess these, they are called "ordinary worldlings possessed of all bonds.
Even if one possesses a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and vows to be born in an evil age to save suffering sentient beings, such a thing is impossible. Why?
Because in an evil world, the objects of the afflictions are powerful; lacking the power of patience (*kṣānti*) oneself, the mind follows along with the objects, such as sounds and forms.

Bound as they are, they fall themselves into the three evil realms; how then could they save sentient beings? Even if they should happen to be born among humans, the Noble Path is difficult to attain.
Perhaps through the merit of giving, precepts, and cultivation, they may be born among humans and become kings, ministers, elders, or those of great wealth and power, possessing sovereign freedom.
Yet, even if they encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), they are unwilling to trust or follow them; because of greed, hatred, and negligence, they extensively create [negative karma].
Driven by these various sins and this evil karma, one enters the three miserable realms (trāya) and remains there for immeasurable kalpas;
upon emerging from hell—known as *naraka* in Sanskrit, which translates as "place of suffering" (*kugju*)—one finds oneself beneath the earth. This subterranean prison is called "earth-hell."
To receive the body of a poor and lowly person, fail to encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), and fall back into hell—such is this cycle of saṃsāra that continues until today;
every person is like this, and this is called the "difficult path" (duṣkaracaryā). Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"If one cannot save oneself when ill, how can one save those who are sick? Furthermore, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra says: "It is like two people..."

Each had relatives who were being swept away by the water; one person, in a state of urgent distress, entered the water directly to rescue them, but because he lacked the skillful means to support them, both he and they sank.
Another person, possessing skillful means, went toward a boat or raft.
Those in the south call it a *pi*, while those in the north call it a raft; this refers to a structure woven from bamboo and wood that floats upon the Ganges River to transport people and goods.
By means of it, those who board and are rescued are all delivered from the peril of drowning. A bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment is likewise like this.

Because one who has not yet attained the power of patience (*kṣānti*) cannot rescue and deliver sentient beings, it is necessary to remain constantly near the Buddha until one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), at which point one is finally able to save sentient beings, like one who has obtained a boat. As the treatise says: "It is, for example, like an infant."

The *Shiming* states: "When a person first takes birth, they are called an *ārbsa* (infant). The area before the chest is called the *yīng*; because one holds them before the chest to nourish them with milk, they are named an *ārbsa*.
They must not be separated from their mother; if they were separated from their mother, they might fall into a pit or well, or die of thirst for milk, just like a fledgling."
When wings have not yet formed, one must rely on trees and cling to branches, unable to travel far;

only when the feathers and pinions are fully developed (the character *he* [革] under *he* means the long feathers of a bird’s wing) can one fly through the air with ease and without obstruction. Ordinary people lack such power, yet by focusing their mindfulness exclusively on Amitābha Buddha, they will attain samādhi.
Because their karma has been perfected, they will, at the moment of death, gather their thoughts and be reborn with certainty.

Having seen Amitābha Buddha without doubt and realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they return to the triple world riding the vessel of the patience of non-arising to rescue suffering sentient beings and extensively perform Buddha-works with unimpeded freedom; thus, the treatise says:
"They sport in the hells."
Because one enters the prison to rescue those in suffering with sovereign mastery of will, it is called the "Gate of Playful Sport.

When a practitioner is born in that land and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they return to the realm of birth and death to teach and transform beings in the hells who suffer.
For this reason, those who seek birth in the Pure Land should understand this teaching; thus, [it is explained] in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is titled "The Easy Path.
The meaning of the "Easy Path" appears within the fifth doubt.
Regarding the second doubt: Question—The essence of all phenomena is empty.
There are two kinds of dharmas: first, the dharma of mind; second, all dharmas. Both kinds are empty. Regarding the emptiness of the dharma of mind:
although the true mind of sentient beings possesses the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is fundamentally devoid of afflictions.

Because it is devoid of afflictions, it is called "emptiness of essence. Second, regarding the emptiness of dharmas: all dharmas of cause and effect arise from conditions; they are produced through the convergence of conditions.
When conditions disperse, they cease; arising and ceasing follow from conditions. Because conditions lack intrinsic nature, they are said to be empty in essence.
However, this question gains the principle while losing the phenomenon, as it is made manifest within the answer itself.
Originally, all things are unborn, equal, and quiescent; yet now, one abandons this to seek that, aspiring to be born in the Western Pure Land of Amitābha—is this not contrary to principle?
Furthermore, a sutra states: "If you seek a pure land, first purify your own mind;
because the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. How can this be reconciled?
The answer is: There are two meanings to this explanation: first, a general response; second, a specific response. Regarding the general response:

if you say that seeking the Pure Land of Amitābha in the West constitutes abandoning this world to seek that one and is therefore unreasonable, then your own insistence on remaining here and not seeking the West is itself to abandon that [Pure Land] and cling to this [world]; this, too, becomes a sickness and is likewise unreasonable. Furthermore...
They further argue: "I do not seek birth there, nor does he seek to dwell here. This is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Subhūti, if you should conceive such a thought—that one who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speaks of the characteristic of the annihilation of all phenomena—do not conceive such a thought. Why? Because one who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
This does not describe a characteristic of annihilation.

As for the citation of the *Vajracchedikā-sūtra* as proof, in that sutra, Subhūti understands the Buddha’s intention by stating that one should not view the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, by means of these two characteristics;
his meaning is that one does not view him by means of marks, which is a negation (*paryudāsa*) that must be understood as such.
All Tathāgatas are fully endowed with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) as the meaning that expresses and defines their merit;
were it otherwise, one would fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Thus we know that while speaking of characteristics, the myriad phenomena are arrayed yet ultimately unobtainable;
and while discussing the nature (*dharmatā*), the single suchness is quiescent and does not obstruct its following conditions. To speak of *anuttara-bodhi*, it should properly be called *anuttarā*.
*Samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.

Second, regarding the specific answer: as for that which is neither born nor extinguished, within the conditions for birth, all dharmas combine without maintaining their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
even if one seeks the essence of birth, it cannot be found. When this birth occurs, it comes from nowhere; therefore, it is called [unborn].
"Neither arising nor ceasing" means that when all phenomena disperse, they do not maintain their own nature by saying, "I am dispersing and ceasing.

Because at the time of this dispersal and cessation, there is nowhere to which they go, it is said they do not cease. This does not mean that there exists some separate "neither-arising-nor-ceasing" apart from what is produced by causes and conditions;
nor does it mean that one fails to seek birth in the Pure Land and instead calls that "non-arising. Regarding this, a verse in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says: "Because of..."
"I say that dharmas produced through conditions are emptiness, they are also called provisional designations, and they are also the meaning of the Middle Way.
Regarding this verse, the first line refers to the object of contemplation, while the following three lines refer to the subject of contemplation.

The first line is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the second line is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), and the final line is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*). This constitutes the three contemplations within a single mind, contemplating the one truth and the three objects.
It is further said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor are they without cause; therefore, they are said to be unarisen.
This verse refutes the clinging to the four types of origination to clarify non-arising.
Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "Though one knows that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates pure lands and transforms all classes of beings.

The first two phrases clarify that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is signless; the latter two phrases clarify that conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is perfectly manifest—this is true conventionality.
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the myriad distinctions naturally vanish; in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the conventional remains eternally distinct from the ultimate.

It is further said: "Suppose there is a person who constructs a palace; if it relies upon solid ground, it can be built at will without obstruction, but if it relies upon empty space, it can never be completed.
Thus, the Buddhas' teaching of the Dharma always relies upon the two truths, speaking without destroying conventional designations.

The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is such that the ultimate and the conventional are of one limit, their essence and function mutually integrated. It has been thus from the very beginning and is not merely so now.

Because it does not destroy provisional designations, there are distinctions of self and other, and of arising and ceasing; yet because it explains the true reality of all phenomena, it is [that same reality].
Arising and ceasing perish of their own accord; by realizing non-unity, one clarifies non-duality. The Sage attained this meaning:

he spoke of the unchanging within the context of following conditions, and he spoke of the emptiness of essence within the context of the manifestation of phenomena. Those deluded followers have lost this essential point:
they seek non-arising outside of arising and ceasing, and they seek equality outside of differentiation, claiming that this constitutes birth in the Pure Land.
How truly unerring is the non-arising of difference!
The wise person zealously seeks birth in the Pure Land, yet realizes that the essence of birth cannot be apprehended; this is precisely the true vision of non-arising.
This is what is meant by: "Because the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure."
"Mind pure, land pure" has two aspects: first, regarding the intrinsic virtue of self-nature purity;
the mind, in every thought-moment, is the body of the Dharma-nature, and every land and every atom is entirely the Land of Tranquil Light (*sukhāvatī*).
This does not clarify cultivation or realization, nor does it establish stages. Second, regarding the cultivated virtue of purity free from defilement; this refers to the three kinds of pure merit.
Through the sixteen sublime contemplations, by relying on the power of others' vows to arouse confident faith, one abandons this defiled land and is born in that pure realm.
Thus, while these two gates are presented, they ultimately converge at a single point; the cultivation of thought is not confused with the fruit, for cause and effect are clearly distinct.
Fools are bound by birth; upon hearing of "birth," they immediately form the conception of birth, and upon hearing of "non-birth," they immediately form the conception of non-birth.
They do not know that birth is itself non-birth and non-birth is itself birth.

Failing to realize this principle, they arbitrarily dispute right and wrong, harboring anger toward others who seek birth in the Pure Land—how great is their error! Such people are slanderers of the Dharma, possessed of false views and outsiders.
This is the Way.
Third Doubt: Question—The Dharma-nature of all Buddhas of the ten directions and their pure lands is equal, and their merits are likewise equal.
A practitioner universally recollects the merits of all Buddhas to give birth to rebirth in all pure lands; why then do they now focus exclusively on [one Buddha]?
Question: If seeking rebirth in the pure land of a single Buddha contradicts the principle of equality, how can one attain birth in that pure land?
Answer: The pure lands of all Buddhas are indeed equal in reality;

however, because sentient beings have dull faculties and are mostly turbid and distracted, it is difficult to achieve success unless they focus their minds exclusively on a single object through samādhi.
Samādhi is properly called *samāpatti*, which is translated as "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*) or "equipoise" (*děngchí*).

This means that by departing from dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), one is said to be "even" (*sama*), and by causing the mind to abide in a state of one-pointedness, it is said to be "held" (*dhṛti*).
Single-minded recollection of Amitābha Buddha is itself the Samādhi of One Mark; by focusing the mind with single-minded devotion, one attains birth in that land.
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sui-yüan wang-sheng ching) states: "The Bodhisattva Puguang asked the Buddha:

'World-Honored One, since there are pure lands throughout the ten directions, for what reason do you exclusively praise the Western Pure Land of Amitābha and specifically dispatch beings to be reborn there? The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Puguang:"
"All sentient beings of Jambudvīpa.
*Jambu* is correctly translated as "Jambū," which is the name of a tree; because there is a Jambū tree on the southern side of this continent, it is named after it.
*Dvīpa* here means "continent."

Because the mind is often turbid and distracted, for this reason, the Western Pure Land of a single Buddha is specially praised, so that sentient beings may concentrate their minds on a single object and thus easily attain rebirth there.
Furthermore, those who contemplate all Buddhas generally find that when the objects of mindfulness are numerous, the mind becomes turbid, scattered, and lax;
because samādhi is difficult to achieve, they cannot attain rebirth. Therefore, one should seek the merit of a single Buddha.
Because they share the same Buddha-nature (*dharmatā*), there is no difference between the merits of all Buddhas;
thus, to recollect Amitābha Buddha is to recollect all Buddhas, and to be born in one pure land is to be born in all pure lands.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The bodies of all Buddhas are the body of a single Buddha; they are one mind, one wisdom, one power, and one fearlessness."

It is likewise. "Power" refers to the ten powers: first, the power of the possible and the impossible; second, the power of the knowledge of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration; fourth, the power of the faculties;

fifth, the power of aspiration; sixth, the power of disposition; seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives; ninth, the power of the divine eye; [and tenth, the power of the exhaustion of outflows].

The ten powers include the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*) and the fearlessnesses, which are the four intrepidities (*vaiśāradya*): first, the intrepidity regarding omniscience;

second, the intrepidity regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, the intrepidity regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path; and fourth, the intrepidity regarding the teaching on the path to the exhaustion of suffering.
It is further said: "For example, just as the pure full moon universally reflects in all waters, and though its reflections are infinite, the original moon neither increases nor decreases;
so too, when unimpeded wisdom is perfected, one achieves equal enlightenment and manifests Buddha-bodies in all lands without duality.
Those with wisdom understand this through analogy; if those with wisdom can penetrate the nature of all moon-reflections, [they will realize the truth]."
The reflection of one moon is the reflection of all moons, for there is no duality in reflections.

Thus, one Buddha is all Buddhas, and all Buddhas are one Buddha, for the Dharma-body is non-dual. Therefore, when one intensely recollects one Buddha, it is simultaneously the recollection of all Buddhas.

Question: It may be that the Dharma-body and the serene light are equal; however, how can the three lands—the mountains, hills, mounds, and pits of this world, and the jeweled trees and flower ponds of the West—be equal as retributive responses?
Answer: The Dharma-body is the essence (*tattva*), while the two bodies (the Reward-body and Transformation-body) are its function (*vṛtti*).
The serene light is the essence, while the three lands are its function. Since these lands are the function of the essence, they are pure or defiled accordingly.

Since it is the very substance of that which is being employed, it is of one flavor and equal; moreover, purity and defilement reside in the capacity of the recipient, not in the Teacher who transforms them.
Thus, the *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma) states:

"As the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, some saw the Buddha in the form of a śramaṇa, some saw the Buddha with the majestic marks and signs of a great being, and others saw the Buddha seated upon a precious lotus flower preaching the Mind-Ground."
In this Dharma-gate, one may see the Buddha’s body as being like empty space, without boundaries or marks;
or one may see the city of Kauśāmbī with its earth, stones, trees, and forests; or see it adorned with the seven treasures;
or see the places where the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time travel and dwell; or see it as the true mark of *tathatā*, the realm of pure Buddhahood.

The Fourth Doubt: Question—Since these [practices] are all mindful recollections for seeking rebirth in the pure land of a single Buddha, why not seek rebirth in the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions by being mindful of any one of them?
Why is it necessary to focus exclusively on the Western Pure Land of Amitābha Buddha?

The answer is: Ordinary people lack wisdom and do not dare to act independently; rather, they rely exclusively on the Buddha’s words, which enable them to focus their thoughts single-mindedly on Amitābha Buddha.

How can it be said that the Buddha’s words do not support this? Throughout the various places where the Great Teacher Śākyamuni preached during his entire lifetime, he consistently exhorted sentient beings to concentrate their minds and focus their thoughts single-mindedly on Amitābha Buddha.
*Amitābha* is translated here as "Immeasurable Life Buddha" (*Wúliàngshòu Fó*), and this refers to the Awakened One (*Jùzhě*).
Those who seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Xīfāng Jílè Shìjiè*) should follow the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* (*Wúliàngshòu jīng*).
This sūtra consists of two fascicles and was translated during the Cao Wei dynasty by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Sengkai; it elucidates the Buddha Amitābha.
Regarding "In the past, the bhikṣu Dharmākara encountered the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and made forty-eight vows":
this refers to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (also known as the *Contemplation Sūtra*). This single-fascicle scripture was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śrīmitra of the Song Dynasty.
Translated by [Yijing], this is the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth), in which the World-Honored One expounds the three types of pure karma and sixteen practices for Lady Vaidehī.
The *Kaiyuan lu* titles it the *Wuliangshou youbotishe* (Commentary on the Infinite Life); this treatise consists of one fascicle and was composed by Vasubandhu.
The author of this [treatise] was Vasubandhu;
he and others, numbering over several dozen, diligently instructed through various sūtras and śāstras, exhorting one to be born in the Western Land, and thus it is a matter of focused mindfulness.
Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha possesses a distinct set of forty-eight great compassionate vows to welcome and guide sentient beings. Moreover, [the text continues:]...

The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that Amitābha Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand marks, each mark having eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*lakṣaṇa*), and each secondary sign emitting eighty-four thousand rays of light that illuminate all worlds.

He gathers in and never abandons those sentient beings who mindfully recite his name; if there is one who recites, their capacity and the Buddha’s response correspond, and they will certainly attain birth [in the Pure Land]. Furthermore, regarding Amitābha...
The *Sūtra of the Minor Amitābha* (translated by Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva), the *Mahā-amitāyur-dhyāna-sūtra*, the *Dhāraṇī of King Drum-Sound*, and others— these sūtras,
translated during the Liang dynasty with the translator's name lost, enable one to recite the *Dhāraṇī of Drum-Sound* and thereby attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (*An-yang*).
It is said that when Śākyamuni Buddha preached this sutra, all the Buddhas of the ten directions— each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—

It is evident that there is no need for doubt; for instance, during the lifetime of Śākyamuni Buddha, there were as many sentient beings who saw the Buddha yet failed to attain the fruits of sainthood as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, states: "In the city of Śrāvastī, there were nine hundred million households;
three hundred million saw the Buddha, three hundred million heard of him but did not see him, and three hundred million neither heard of nor saw him.

If it was thus in Śrāvastī, other countries may be known by the same principle. As for 'Ganges' (*gaṅgā*), this is properly the name of a river deity, which has come to serve as the name of the river itself."
From Lake Anavatapta flow four great rivers; this river is the one that issues from the Silver Ox Mouth on the eastern side.

The lake measures forty *li* on each of its four sides and contains abundant, fine sand. Because the Buddha frequently stayed near this lake to preach the Dharma, he often took its features as metaphors whenever he spoke.
It is the same when Maitreya appears in the world: there are many who do not attain the fruits of sainthood, yet they are not like those in Amitābha’s Pure Land;

as soon as one is born in that land, all have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and not a single person has ever fallen back into the triple world to be bound by the karma of birth and death.
Furthermore, I have heard from traditions in the Western Regions that there were three bodhisattvas: the first was named Asaṅga, the second was named... [text fragment].
Vasubandhu had three masters, one of whom was Siṃhabuddhi. These three men were of like mind and made a vow to be reborn together in Tuṣita to behold Maitreya.
It was their promise that whoever died first would see Maitreya and return to inform the others. Siṃhabuddhi passed away first; he had been gone for several years without returning.
Later, when Vasubandhu was about to pass away, Asaṅga said to him: "Have you seen Maitreya?"
He immediately came to inform [Asaṅga] that Vasubandhu had departed; it was only after three years had passed that he returned. Asaṅga asked, "For what reason have you taken so much time to return?
Vasubandhu replied, "When I arrived in that heaven, I listened to Maitreya Bodhisattva deliver a single session of Dharma.
Having circumambulated him, I immediately came back to inform you; this is because the days in that heaven are long."
Fifty human years constitute one day and night in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; one hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
two hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Yāma Heaven; four hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Tuṣita Heaven;
eight hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
One thousand six hundred years [of the human realm] constitutes one day and night for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.
Therefore, three years have already passed here. When asked where Siṃhabuddhi was now, Vasubandhu replied:
"Siṃhabuddhi has gone out to enjoy the pleasures of the five desires as a celestial being; since he departed with his retinue, [it has been this long]."
Since it is not seen that even the minor bodhisattvas who are born there still cling to the five desires, how much less so for ordinary beings?

Therefore, those who make this vow to be born in the Pure Land of the West will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression; because they are free from such obstacles, they do not seek birth in Tuṣita.
The Eighth Doubt: Question—Sentient beings have, since beginningless time, created immeasurable karma;
yet in this present life, they possess but a single form, do not encounter virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and furthermore commit every kind of sinful deed, leaving no evil uncommitted.

How can it be that at the moment of death, the accomplishment of ten recitations immediately leads to rebirth in the Pure Land and the transcendence of the karmic fetters of the triple world? How can this matter be reconciled?
The commentary states: Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been unable to know the quantity or the strength and weakness of their seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma.

These seeds of the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—are maintained by the ālayavijñāna and do not perish; they cannot be overturned or destroyed except by uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.
It is not only the seeds of the seven branches of wholesome and unwholesome action of body and speech that do not perish, but also those on the mental level.
In these three matters, you should be even more cautious and diligently cultivate meditative practice so that evil thoughts do not arise.

Therefore, in the *Wei wu sanmei jing* (The Scripture on the Samādhi of Non-Existence), the Buddha told Ānanda: "The reason people born in the human realm fail to attain the Way is simply because they sit amidst a multitude of defiled thoughts.
One thought comes and one thought goes; in a single day and night, there are eight hundred and forty million [thoughts]."

If among tens of millions of thoughts not a single wholesome thought ceases, one will obtain a wholesome retribution; if a single unwholesome thought arises, one will obtain an unwholesome retribution.
Like an echo responding to a sound, or a shadow following a form—who upon hearing this would not be startled and awakened?
Even tainted wholesome states should not be allowed to arise, let alone unwholesome thoughts.
Those who are able to encounter a virtuous friend at the moment of death and achieve the ten recitations do so because of their wholesome karma from previous lives.

If one's wholesome karma is strong, the ten recitations will be achieved; however, for those with much unwholesome karma, they cannot even meet a virtuous friend, let alone achieve the ten recitations.
Since your own unwholesome karma from beginningless time has been heavy, the ten recitations at the moment of death [are difficult to accomplish].
Regarding those that are light, their relative weight is now evaluated through three principles; it is not fixed by time, duration, or quantity.
What are these three? First, that which resides in the mind; second, that which resides in conditions; and third, that which resides in determination. As for "residing in the mind":
when one commits an offense, it arises from one's own deluded and inverted mind; whereas the mind that recollects the Buddha arises from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When one hears the teaching of the true merits and name of Amitābha Buddha, how could a single thought of emptiness and a single thought of reality be compared?
It is like a dark room ten thousand years old where the darkness is instantly dispelled as soon as the sunlight arrives;

how could it be that the long-standing darkness refuses to be extinguished? As for those conditioned by circumstances, at the time they commit offenses, they do so from a mind conditioned by the darkness of false ignorance.
The realm of falsehood arises from perversion.
The realm of falsehood refers to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and so forth.
The mind that recollects the Buddha arises from hearing the name of the Buddha’s pure and true merits as a condition for supreme enlightenment.
When the mind gives rise to one that is true and one that is false, how can they be compared? It is like a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow;

the poison is so fierce and cruel that it wounds the flesh and penetrates to the bone. Yet, upon hearing the sound of a drum for the medicine that eliminates it, the arrow immediately comes out and the poison is removed.
How could one refuse to have it removed simply because the poison was deep? For those established in certainty, at the very moment they commit a transgression, [the remedy] is already present.
There is an interval between the preceding mind and the succeeding mind.
Regarding the existence of an interval and a succeeding mind prior to the end of life, if one commits evil at the point of death, there is no interval and no succeeding mind;
yet the retribution summoned is still grave. Therefore, the text below states: "If, at the moment of death, one gives rise to a single thought of resolute false view, one falls into the Avīci Hell."
Regarding the Avīci Hell:
at the time of recollecting the Buddha, one possesses an uninterrupted mind (*anantara-citta*) and no subsequent mind.

At the moment of death, when powerful roots of goodness arise such that no further evil can intervene, this is called the "uninterrupted mind" (*anantara-citta*). This refers to the recollection of the Buddha at the time of death.
When the Buddha relinquished his life-span, he had no further thoughts remaining thereafter; this is called the "mind without succession.

He then immediately cast off his life with such fierce and sharp wholesome intent that he was reborn instantly—just as a rope ten spans in circumference cannot be severed by a thousand men, yet a youth wielding a sword can split it in two in an instant.
The "rope" is a metaphor for beginningless evil karma; the "ten fathoms" refers to the multitude of thousands, meaning ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Ordinary worldlings cannot subdue the "youth," which is a metaphor for the practitioner at the initial stage of the path. Wielding the sword, he achieves accomplishment in ten recitations;
"in a moment, it is divided into two" means that as soon as one extends or contracts the arm, one abandons this life and is born in that [other] state.
Furthermore, it is like a thousand-year-old pile of firewood that is completely consumed in a short time by a fire of large beans.

Although this eighth question-and-answer pair clarifies that karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) necessarily involve afflictions (*kleśa*), and that afflictions are merely synonyms for karma, the "firewood" is a metaphor for the afflictions;
"thousand years" refers to the beginningless [past]; the "large" refers to wisdom; and the "single bean" refers to the most minimal [amount].
When a practitioner hears the exhortations and transformations of a virtuous friend, they come to know and develop deep faith;

upon reaching the stage of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), their afflictions are suddenly exhausted, and rebirth in the Pure Land becomes certain. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Afflictions are like food and drink, which cause all my disciples to manifest a craving for them."

Furthermore, it is like a person who, throughout their entire life, has cultivated the ten wholesome karmas and ought to be reborn in heaven, yet at the moment of death gives rise to a single thought of resolute wrong view and immediately falls into the Avīci Hell.

Because such evil karma is so violent and sharp, it is able to displace—even to the point of pushing aside and removing—the wholesome karma of a lifetime, causing one to fall into an evil realm; how much more so when [such a state of mind persists] at the time of death?

It is impossible for a mind of intense intensity that recollects the Buddha with true and uninterrupted virtuous karma not to dispel beginningless evil karma and thereby attain birth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, it is said that a single moment of mindfulness of the Buddha extinguishes the heavy offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death;

when one recollects the Buddha with such a mind of intense intensity, evil karma is suppressed and extinguished, and one will certainly attain birth [in the Pure Land] without needing [further effort].
Regarding the doubt that the ancient tradition of judging the accomplishment of ten recitations to be intended for another time—that this [interpretation] is untenable—how is this known?
The *Śrāvakabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (She lun) states: "It is solely by virtue of making a vow, and there is no practice whatsoever. The *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* (Za ji lun) states:
"If one has the vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, one immediately attains rebirth therein. Furthermore, if a person hears the name of the Buddha Vimalacandra...
To claim that those who immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do so solely through causes from a different time, while possessing no practice whatsoever,
and to interpret the "ten recitations" of the final moment as being intended for a different time— how great is such an error!
I pray that all practitioners will reflect deeply on this principle, fortify their own minds, and not fall into self-destruction by trusting in divergent views.

Regarding the "intention" (*abhiprāya*) at that time, the sixth chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, titled "The Chapter on Manifesting the Intention," explains four kinds of intention:
first, the intention of equality; second, the intention of another time; third, the intention of another meaning; and fourth, the intention of the inclinations of sentient beings.
Among these, regarding the second, the intention of another time, it states: "By merely making a vow, one will go to the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and attain rebirth there."
Regarding the statement that "birth" refers to a discourse on a different time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*), the Master himself explained it as follows:

"For example, by means of a single coin, one seeks and obtains a thousand coins; these are not obtained in a single day, but are obtained through a different time. The intention of the Tathāgata is likewise:
this single coin serves as the cause for the thousand coins, and making a vow serves as the cause for rebirth. Thus spoke the Great Master Zhiyi.

The meaning is as follows: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that one must specifically make a vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, while the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states that one attains Bodhi merely by hearing the Buddha’s name.
These two treatises do not mention "practice" at all; this is the sense of the "different time" (*anyakāla*).

The ancient masters erroneously judged even the ten recitations of the fierce and sharp wholesome practice to be of the "different time" type, and thus [the author] refutes them. Now, if one wishes to be born in the Pure Land:
Now, it is necessary that both practice and vows be fully perfected: if there is practice without vows, the practice has no source;
if there are vows without practice, the vows yield no attainment. When practice and vows support one another, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.
The Ninth Doubt: Question—Since the Western Land is ten trillion Buddha-fields away from here, how can ordinary beings, who are weak and inferior, possibly reach it?

Furthermore, the *Treatise on Rebirth* states: "Women and those with impaired faculties (impaired faculties meaning those with deficiencies or defects, such as the blind, the deaf, the mute, and the dumb), and those of the two vehicles, are not born there.
Given these sacred teachings, one must know that women and those with impaired faculties certainly cannot [be reborn there].
One attains rebirth there.
The answer is: this is spoken in contrast to the ordinary person’s physical eye and the mental capacity of birth-and-death.

Although the Western Land is ten trillion *kṣetras* away from here, for any sentient being who has perfected the karma for the Pure Land, the mind of meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the Pure Land.

The very movement of thought within the mind that aspires for rebirth is itself the moment of birth in the Pure Land. To this effect, the *Contemplation Sutra* states: "The land of Amitābha Buddha is not far from here.
Furthermore, the power of karma is inconceivable; one may attain birth there in a single thought-moment without needing to worry about distance.
It is like a person in a dream: although the body remains on the bed, the mind, intellect, and consciousness [are elsewhere].

The mind is divided into the true and the false, comprising three types: first, that which is exclusively true, namely the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*), which has been serene and eternally abiding from the very beginning, possessing spiritual understanding and luminous illumination unlike wood or stone;

second, the union of the true and the false, namely the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*); and third, that which is exclusively false, namely the preceding seven consciousnesses. Thus, the first is the essence, while the latter two are its manifestations.

Furthermore, regarding the terms *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*: that which accumulates and records is called *citta*, namely the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), because it accumulates seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

That which cogitates is called *manas*, namely the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*), because it grasps the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as an internal self and gives rise to the four afflictions.
That which discriminates is called *vijñāna*, namely the preceding six consciousnesses, because they differentiate the six sense-objects (*viṣaya*).
Within this context, only the sixth consciousness is selected because it universally perceives the ten directions and the three periods of time;
since the sixth necessarily depends on the seventh, and the seventh necessarily depends on the eighth, they are collectively termed "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).
They reach all worlds in other directions as if nothing had changed from their ordinary lives; birth in the Pure Land is likewise.
One reaches it the moment a thought arises—there is no need for doubt. As for women and those with impaired faculties, and those of the two vehicles who are not born there:
this merely refers to the fact that there are no women in that land, nor any who are blind, deaf, or mute. It does not mean that the women of this world do not go there.
If one were to say that those with physical deficiencies cannot be reborn there, such a statement would be foolish and entirely fail to grasp the meaning of the sutra.
For instance, Lady Vaidehī was the principal petitioner for rebirth in the Pure Land, and she, along with five hundred female attendants,
received a prediction from the Buddha that they would all attain rebirth in that land.
According to the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*: "Good sons and good daughters, if there are those with faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land.

According to the *Lotus Sūtra*: "If, during the five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there is a woman who hears this sūtra and practices according to its teachings, upon the end of her life here, she shall immediately go to peace."

It is known for certain that women here will surely attain rebirth in that world, dwelling amidst the assembly of Great Bodhisattvas surrounding Amitābha Buddha, born within lotus flowers upon jeweled thrones.
However, in this place, women, as well as those who are blind, deaf, or mute, if they bring to mind Amitābha Buddha, will all be reborn in that land;

once reborn, they shall no longer receive a female body nor a body with impaired faculties. As for those of the two vehicles, if they merely turn their minds and vow to be born in the Pure Land, upon reaching there, they will no longer harbor the attachments of the two vehicles.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the grasping at a self has been exhausted and one no longer receives further existence; it is not said that there are further places of birth.
That the present text speaks of "turning back" (*pariṇāmanā*) with the vow to be born [there] is the meaning of the Mahāyāna.

The *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* says that the Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, while the *Treatise on Rebirth* (*Sukhāvatīvyūhopadeśa*) states that there are no followers of the two vehicles under that Buddha.

Since the manifestation for the sake of those with various capacities reveals both coarse and subtle aspects: the coarse aspect refers to the *nirmāṇa-kṣetra* (transformation land), which includes the two vehicles;

the subtle aspect refers to the *paranirmita-upabhoga-kṣetra* (land of others' enjoyment), which consists exclusively of bodhisattvas. This transformation land not only contains śrāvakas but also women;
as the *Drum-Svara-rāja Sūtra* states: "The father of Amitābha Buddha is named Candrottara, and his mother is named Viśeṣavatī."

The meaning of "supreme and wondrous countenance" appears to contradict [the literal sense], yet in reality it accords with the principle; other meanings are as explained in the title of the *Śāstra* and within the sixth section on doubts.
For this reason, it is said that women and those with impaired faculties do not give rise to the lineage of the Two Vehicles, but this does not mean that women [are excluded] from this place.
Furthermore, those with impaired faculties cannot be born there; thus, the Forty-Eight Vows of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* state:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, any woman in the worlds of the ten directions should call upon my name and, loathing her female body, should receive another female body after the end of her life, may I not attain perfect enlightenment—how much less could one be born in that land and yet receive another female body?"
The same applies to those with impaired faculties.

Tenth, Doubt: Question—Now, desiring to resolve the matter of rebirth in the Western Land, I do not yet know what practices one should perform, nor what should serve as the seed for attaining birth in that land.
Furthermore, ordinary laypeople all have wives and children and have not severed their lustful desires.
If one asks whether it is possible to be born there, the answer is: those who are determined to attain rebirth in the Western Land will certainly be born there by means of two types of practice.
First is the practice of revulsion and detachment; second is the practice of joyful aspiration. Regarding the practice of revulsion and detachment:
since beginningless time, ordinary beings have been bound by the five desires and have transmigrated through the five realms of existence.
When expanded, there are six realms (*ṣadgati*), but because the asuras are subsumed within the realm of hungry ghosts (*pretagati*), they are combined into five realms.
These beings undergo all manner of suffering yet do not give rise to a mind of revulsion; they do not depart from the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) and have no prospect of escape.
For this reason, one should constantly contemplate this body as pus, blood, excrement, urine, and all other foul secretions—impure and putrid. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "This..."
The rakshasa of physical ignorance dwells within it; what wise person would take pleasure in this body? Furthermore, a sutra says:
"This body is a collection of manifold sufferings; everything about it is impure, a constriction, a festering ulcer, and so forth."
The *Erya* states that "yoke" (*e*) means a crossbar; it refers to that which is placed transversely at the end of the shaft to press against the neck of the ox.
In its current form, it is called the *yuan*. Ordinary people are bound by afflictions (*kleśa*), their fundamental state being like that of an ox constrained by a yoke.
From the fundamental lack of benefit up to the bodies of the various devas, it is likewise so for all.

Whether walking or sitting, whether awake or aware, the practitioner should constantly contemplate this body as being only suffering and devoid of pleasure, thereby giving rise to a profound sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*).

Even if one cannot suddenly sever attachment to a wife or household, one should gradually cultivate weariness by practicing the seven contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*): first, contemplating this body of lustful desire.
That which arises from the affliction of greed is precisely the impurity of the seed.
Since afflictions moisten karma to bring about retribution, one knows that afflictions serve as the seeds for the body of retribution.
Second, at the time of the parents' union, when the red and white elements combine, consciousness takes rebirth within them;
this is the impurity of conception.
When the two drops combine and consciousness takes rebirth therein, at the very first stage of the *kalala*.
Third, while in the mother’s womb, one dwells between the receptacle for the fetus (*āśaya*) below and the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*) above; this is impurity of dwelling.
Fourth, while in the mother’s womb, one consumes only the mother’s blood; this is impurity of consumption.
Fifth, when the months and days are complete, the head turns toward the birth canal and one emerges amidst pus and blood, foul and chaotic; this is impurity of initial birth. Sixth.
That which is covered by a thin skin, yet within its interior pus and blood pervade every place—this is the impurity of the entire body.
Seventh, even after death, when it becomes bloated and putrid, with bones and flesh scattered in all directions as solitary wolves devour it—this is ultimate impurity.
One's own body is likewise so; one should cultivate a profound sense of weary detachment toward beloved objects, such as the bodies of men and women, at all times.
Regarding the contemplation of impurity: if one can contemplate the body's impurity in this manner, the afflictions of sensual desire will gradually diminish.
Furthermore, one should practice the ten contemplations (*daśa-saṃjñā*).
The ten contemplations are: first, the contemplation of impermanence; second, the contemplation of suffering; third, the contemplation of non-self; fourth, the contemplation of the impurity of food.

5. The perception of the world as unattractive; 6. the perception of death; 7. the perception of impurity; 8. the perception of abandonment; 9. the perception of detachment; 10. the perception of cessation.
Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes the nine perceptions, which constitute the Great Contemplation of Impurity (*mahā-aśubha-bhāvanā*).

These nine perceptions are: 1. the perception of bloating; 2. the perception of disintegration; 3. the perception of being smeared with blood; 4. the perception of festering pus; 5. the perception of bluish discoloration.
Sixth, the perception of consumption; seventh, the perception of scattering; eighth, the perception of bones;

ninth, the perception of burning—these are explained in detail as set forth in the sūtras. Furthermore, one makes this vow: "May I forever depart from the impure, fetid, and putrid food of the three realms, from the bodies of men and women that are enmeshed in the five desires;
may I attain the Dharma-nature body of the Pure Land. This is called revulsion and detachment.
Regarding the practice of aspiring through joyful longing, there are further two types: first, clarifying the intention for seeking rebirth;
second, contemplating the adornments and other features of that Pure Land. As for the intention for seeking rebirth through joyful longing, it is as follows:
one contemplates within oneself that the reason for seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is the desire to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from suffering. Thus, one reflects:
I now lack the power; if I remain in this evil age where the conditions of affliction are powerful, I will be bound by my own karma and submerged in the three miserable realms for many kalpas.
Thus revolving in this cycle since beginningless time, never resting, when shall I be able to rescue suffering sentient beings?
For this reason, I seek birth in the Pure Land to draw near to the Buddhas, so that once I have realized the Dharma of non-arising, [I may fulfill this vow].
Only through patience can one rescue suffering sentient beings within this degenerate age; thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* states:
"To speak of generating the bodhicitta is precisely the mind that aspires to become a Buddha. The mind that aspires to become a Buddha is the mind that seeks to deliver sentient beings.
The mind that seeks to deliver sentient beings is the mind that embraces sentient beings so they may be born in the Buddha-land. Furthermore, one must aspire to be born in the Pure Land.
To possess these two practices, first, one must distance oneself from the three obstacles to the Dharma-gate of Bodhi;
second, one must attain the three factors conducive to Bodhi. What are the three obstacles to the Dharma-gate of Bodhi?
First, relying on the gate of wisdom, one does not seek personal pleasure, thereby distancing oneself from the egoistic mind and its attachment to one's own body.

Ordinary beings sink into the cycle of the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence because they are attached to the self and what belongs to the self, thereby being unable to cultivate the practice of renunciation.
"Self" refers to the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*), while "what belongs to the self" refers to the secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Second, by relying on the gate of compassion, one uproots the suffering of all sentient beings and abandons the mind that remains indifferent toward those who lack peace;
third, by relying on the gate of skillful means, one constantly feels pity for all sentient beings, desiring to grant them happiness, and abandons the mind that seeks honor and offerings for oneself.
If one can distance oneself from these three obstacles to the Dharma of enlightenment, one will attain the three [bodies].
One plants the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
These three types of factors conducive to enlightenment correspond respectively to the reversal of the three aforementioned obstacles to enlightenment;
thus, the first type pertains to one’s own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*), while the latter two pertain to the transformation of others (*parārtha*).
First is the undefiled pure mind, which does not seek various pleasures for oneself.
The above is the text of the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth), and the following is the commentary by the Great Master Zhiyi.
This is the state of undefiled purity; if one seeks rebirth for one's own sake, it defiles one's own mind and obstructs the gateway to Bodhi.
Therefore, the undefiled and pure mind is the second gateway to conforming with bodhi: it is the pure mind of tranquility, for the sake of uprooting the suffering of sentient beings.
(The upper part is the treatise; the lower part is the commentary. Bodhi is the place of purity where all sentient beings find peace.
If one does not resolve to uproot all sentient beings and cause them to leave the suffering of birth and death, one violates the gateway to bodhi; therefore, there is the pure mind of tranquility.
These three are the gates of conforming to Bodhi, which consist of the joy of a pure mind; this is because one desires to cause all sentient beings to attain Great Bodhi.
(The above is the treatise; the below is the commentary. Bodhi is the place of ultimate, eternal bliss.
If one does not resolve to cause all sentient beings to attain ultimate, eternal bliss, one violates the gate of Bodhi. How, then, can the causes of this Bodhi be obtained?

Having been born in the Pure Land, one never leaves the Buddha and attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thereafter, within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one rescues suffering sentient beings with the perfect integration of compassion and wisdom.
This perfect integration of compassion and wisdom is the practice of non-abiding; because of compassion, one does not abide in *nirvāṇa*. How could this be the same as that of the Lesser Vehicle?

Because they are mounted upon wisdom, they do not abide in birth and death; how could they be the same as ordinary beings? When the internal mind possesses both [aspects] and does not employ one to the exclusion of the other, it is called "perfect interfusion" (yuanrong).
It is stable yet constantly functional, sovereign and unimpeded.
The perfectly interfused fundamental mind, the wondrously luminous true nature, is the non-duality of quiescence and wisdom; its essence and attributes are directly integrated.

While ordinary beings turn their backs on awakening and wander astray, the various sages return to the source and attain sovereignty. Thus, they are able to remain unmoved within the limit of reality while appropriately deploying great compassion;
their manifestation and concealment are not constant, and their quiescent function is unimpeded.
This is precisely the bodhicitta; this is the intent of the vow for rebirth. Second, regarding the clarification of the mind that aspires and seeks:

the aspiring mind gives rise to thoughts by taking Amitābha Buddha as its object—whether as the *dharmakāya*, the *saṃbhogakāya*, or the *nirmāṇakāya*—with his golden radiance, the eighty-four thousand marks, each mark possessing eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), and each secondary sign emitting eighty-four thousand [rays of light].
A thousand rays of light constantly illuminate the Dharma-realm, gathering in those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha;

furthermore, one contemplates the adornments of the seven treasures of that Pure Land in detail, as described in the *Sixteen Contemplations* of the *Contemplation Sūtra*, and constantly practices the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
Regarding the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*): both mental visualization and the oral recitation of the name are termed "Buddha-recitation.

Yet, various sutras and śāstras clearly explain that through two practices one may attain the Way: first, non-mindfulness (*amanasikāra*), and second, mindfulness (*manasikāra*). First, as for non-mindfulness, this is the *tathatā-samādhi*.
One must simply remain alert and tranquil, not giving rise to攀緣 (*pān-yuan*, object-seeking attachment), so that the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) manifests.

When subject and object are both extinguished through mutual correspondence, even this mind is extinguished; unlike the great void, it is only by settling the mind in this way that one can harmonize with the Way.

The *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) states: "With thought, one falls into the net of Māra; without thought, one immediately attains liberation. Because the mind moves, it is not the Way;
because it is unmoving, it is the Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*). The *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith) states: "If one attains non-thought, then one is heading toward [enlightenment]."
Because of the Buddha’s wisdom, those who possess these two forms of mindfulness are practicing the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.

They maintain mental images of the Buddha’s three bodies (*trikāya*) and his immeasurable merits, as well as the pure adornments of his environment and requisites, with single-minded focus and without distraction.

When this visualization is perfected, they likewise attain visions of the Buddha and awaken to the path of practice, as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*.

In the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises, contemporary students value only "mindfulness-free" (*amanasikāra*) practice while remaining ignorant of those who cultivate the path through "mindfulness" (*manasikāra*).
You must earnestly examine yourself within these two approaches to determine which practice accords with your own disposition; do not mistakenly praise or disparage the words of the Sages.

Just as a person drinking water knows for themselves whether it is cold or warm, do not blindly follow others by placing empty emphasis on "mindfulness-free" practice alone. Furthermore, [the text continues:]

Unable to sit upright in meditative composure, one’s myriad sensory objects collapse; though one may momentarily cease the攀緣 (pān-yuan, mental proliferations), one cannot avoid dwelling in the dullness of the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The six sense-faculties are in turmoil, the three poisons blaze fiercely, and one indulges in manifold false speech to deceive the ignorant laity.

By simplistically rejecting the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and arbitrarily fabricating right and wrong, one destroys the roots of goodness in others—a sin that could not be greater. Rebirth in the Pure Land... [is thus jeopardized].
The path is level at dawn and easy to traverse; I exhort future generations to carefully distinguish the true from the false, lest they waste their lives in vain.

Furthermore, all virtuous deeds performed—such as the giving of gifts and the observance of precepts—are dedicated to all sentient beings with the shared vow to be born in that land, so that birth there may be certain. This is called the Gate of Aspiration.
